title: Mining taxes; Sunshine Mine disaster; miners' wives
description: Laura Williamson begins by commenting on Idaho's lack of a severance tax on mining companies and discusses a Boise State study interviewing wives of Sunshine Mine disaster survivors. She recommends potential interviewees among local miners' wives and recalls the 1972 fire in which 91 men died, describing how she sat up nursing her baby listening to radio reports and crying. Dale Anderson asks for names of women willing to be interviewed.

title: Personal data; leaving and returning to Kellogg; small town gossip
description: Anderson collects basic personal data from Williamson, who was born in Kellogg in 1941. Williamson explains that she moved away after high school, lived in New Mexico and Tacoma, and cried about returning when her husband got a job in Kellogg. She describes disliking small-town gossip and discusses differences in how men and women gossip.

title: Air pollution; lead contamination; landscape change
description: Williamson describes severe SO2 air pollution and lead contamination from the Bunker Hill smelter, including burnt vegetation, health precautions for children, and friends who have moved away. She recounts how mining timber cutting, a fire, and sheep grazing stripped the hills, and notes that many Bunker Hill workers' families live in Coeur d'Alene because wives refuse to live in Kellogg.

title: Family background; parents and siblings
description: Anderson gathers detailed family information. Williamson gives her parents' names, birth dates and places, her mother's work as a homemaker and lunch program janitor, her father's work as a mechanic, and the names and ages of her two brothers and two sisters. She notes her parents moved to Seattle when she was a college sophomore.

title: Husband; marriage; college graduation
description: Williamson discusses her husband, a teacher with a master's degree in geography, and their June 1963 wedding in Moscow held the same day as her college graduation. She describes being far more excited about the marriage than the graduation, their subsequent move to New Mexico as a honeymoon, and having known each other two or three years. She notes she had originally planned to be a career person.

title: Children; childbirth; household skills
description: Williamson talks about her two sons, including a breech birth and waiting in labor due to poor insurance, and the decision to have no more children. She lists her skills in canning, sewing, and recycling, describing how she reuses jeans, cans, and poster board, and mentions bike riding, snowshoeing, and reupholstering furniture.

title: Work history; teaching; casework
description: Williamson recounts her employment history: waitressing at Cougar Mountain Lodge, cooking for the British Consulate during the Seattle World's Fair, marketing home milk dispensers in Denver, teaching science in Gallup, New Mexico, working for a dishonest freezer food company in Albuquerque, and serving as a welfare caseworker helping women return to work and school. She describes moving back to the Northwest and working in Tacoma before settling in Kellogg.

title: Research work; air monitoring; environmental activism
description: Williamson describes working on the Boise State Sunshine Mine study and a federal flood study on women's attitudes, then helping with a Christmas air-quality monitoring project that required climbing icy rooftops. She discusses testifying at hearings against Bunker Hill, losing friends among those threatened by possible mine closure, and her determination to speak out until her family can move away.

title: Book club; TOPS; health and dieting
description: Williamson describes her book club and her membership in TOPS, where she once lost fifty pounds. She reflects on dieting as her great failure, feels she was smart enough to be a doctor, and discusses concerns about her weight and health, including her desire to work for Bunker Hill to learn what goes on there.

title: Church activities; YMCA volleyball; local outings
description: Williamson talks about church volunteering, Bible school teaching, and volleyball at the YMCA with about twenty women. She describes outings with teachers to the Snake Pit restaurant where the group tried Rocky Mountain oysters, and childhood memories of swimming in the North Fork River before pollution and flooding affected the area.

title: AAUW; awards; church service; scholarships
description: Williamson mentions intermittent AAUW membership, high school scholarships, playing the oboe in band, and church citations for volunteer work. She details the Bunker Hill company scholarships she received as a miner's daughter and being the only recipient to repay the grant-in-aid as promised.

title: Scholarship details; politics; household roles
description: Williamson explains that Bunker Hill scholarships were later restricted by law, and discusses her college job as a cook's helper at Hayes Hall. She considers and rejects running for city council because family takes priority, and describes her husband's refusal to do dishes or ironing and her dismay when her son called kitchen work women's work.

title: Part-time work; television and reading; husband; wanting children
description: Laura Williamson wishes mothers could work part time or share jobs, then describes her television habits including All My Children, Sesame Street, and the Today Show, and her preference for reading. She calls her husband the most loving person she knows and recalls waiting seven years for children, her fear after a neighbor's baby died of crib death, and how much she wanted her first child.

title: Family outings; husband's teaching; children's learning; childbirth
description: She compares her pre-children travels with outings in Coeur d'Alene and trips to Expo '74, prompted partly by the lead discovery. Her husband teaches geography while she, a Home Ec graduate, taught science; she describes answering her children's questions about sex and nature. She recounts learning about childbirth from books, touring the delivery room, and her difficult breech birth.

title: Small town life; childhood food and gardens; family recreation and work ethic
description: She praises Kellogg's neighborhood where mothers watch out for each other's children and her preference for raising children in a small town. She contrasts her childhood eating home-raised rabbits and chickens and working in the garden with her children's upbringing, noting Kellogg's lead-contaminated soil ruins gardens now. She also describes her family's work ethic, where building projects counted as recreation.

title: Household help; siblings; college mischief; prostitution; dolls; canning
description: She discusses ironing, hiring housekeeping help while working full time, and her mother having help despite being poor. Youngest of her family, she recalls her siblings as babysitters, planning her parents' 50th anniversary party, and sneaking beer into the University of Idaho Home Management House. She is untroubled by Wallace's brothels, says her boys rarely play with dolls, and describes canning, freezing, and drying berries.

title: Depression; utilities; environmental concern and lead pollution
description: She retells her father's Depression story of a man eating potato peelings and explains the mining economy kept the area stable. She describes surviving a frozen water main with a sick baby and muddy flood water, and says she is only an environmentalist because of the lead studies, criticizing the smelter and zinc plant and unconcerned residents.

title: Lead test results; college hopes; small town advice; women's lib
description: She compares her family's blood lead levels with official danger thresholds and wants research to continue. She hopes her sons attend college, advises newcomers to small towns to be flexible and tolerant, and explains her ambivalence about women's liberation, supporting choice and equal pay while defending her role at home and recalling a promotion lost to quota hiring at the Albuquerque welfare department.
